p:
So, NYC Cares offers several services, including high-quality mental health and substance abuse services. They also offer a primary care provider, and so that provider can refer individuals to appropriate resources which can include a social worker, a therapist, a psychiatrist. So that we know includes in-person screenings, but as well as virtual health and mental health services. We as MOIA, and I said this previously as well, we continue to encourage New Yorkers to enroll in NYC Cares. All city residents are welcome to apply regardless of immigration status. We– also, I’ll add

one last thing that we also provide NYC Cares fliers at our outreach events that are translated into a variety of languages. We include information in our English language classes. So there are quite a bit of ways that we actually promote NYC Cares and just to encourage the participation.

Perfect. And shifting gears, but kind of staying in line with that, can you talk a little bit about MOIA’s partnership with H+H and how both entities ensure that immigrants are not afraid to seek care?

MOIA and H+H maintain routine communications, and in the past we’ve collaborated on providing policy updates to their teams. Last year, our office worked with H+H and DOHMH to publish an open letter to immigrant New Yorkers, really emphasizing the need for them to seek care, explaining the various options that are available to them as well regardless of status. So we have a good working relationship with H+H. H+H also like many other agencies sits and is part of our– MOIA’s interagency taskforce on immigration. So that is routinely where we share best practices,

changes to policies, things that impact immigrant New Yorkers.

Okay. I mean, I know that, you know, the reality is that we– I really want to make sure that they’re being aggressive about those campaigns, because unfortunately the truth of the matter is that we cannot afford for folks to only be using those services as emergency services, right? We want them to be using them as preventive services and preventive health care, and so I’m really hoping that that is a part of the conversation we’re really getting in front of it. Also, you know, federal public housing requires at least one household member to have an eligible immigration status. However, on February 20th, the US Department of Housing and Urban Development published notice of proposed rule-making that world require immigration for everyone living in HUD assisted housing which will harm mixed-status families. Can you talk a little bit about what steps MOIA has taken to collaborate with NYCHA? We just had our NYCHA hearing yesterday. We asked this question. I asked this question of NYCHA, and while seem empathetic,they are fully funded by the federal government and so it is quite a cause for pause. So,

can you talk a little bit about your collaboration with NYCHA?

Yeah. And specifically as it relates to this proposed change, MOIA is working with NYCHA and other agencies to submit a public comment. In response to the proposed change and I’ll add again that NYCHA also sits on our MOIA’s interagency Taskforce. So, we look forward to kind of– continuing to engage them on how do we respond to this potential change.

Okay. Yeah, I would love to see some, you know, regular policy updates, making sure that they’re aware of that process, and also for them to do maybe a visual campaign. I have 23 NYCHA developments in my district, and I would know if there was one, very clearly. So, I know that 311 is also one of the main ways residents report issues, ask questions about city programming and getting help accessing city services. What is your partnership with 311?

We have a great working relationship with 311. We coordinate with them on calls related to immigration. So, calls that are made to 311 are either routed to our legal services

hotline that’s run by Catholic Charities, or they’re routed to the general MOIA hotline. We engage with 311 on an as-needed basis as well just to address any sort of trends that we may be seeing. Both MOIA’s hotline and the– MOIA’s hotline and our legal services hotline. Also, keep track of calls that are coming in. They can in fact also track those calls and can identify when someone has called from 311 as well.
And–
[interposing] If I may, Chair, add one thing?
Yes, please.

I would also just add to what the Commissioner laid out. We have been very intentional about meeting with them and providing them up-to-date policy changes. So when our website was updated with resources, we ensured to walk them through that. And we have continuously relied on them, too, on best practices and guidance even for our own MOIA legal support hotline. They’ve also flagged– there are– the Commissioner mentioned spikes on specific issues. They report them to us,

and we work with them to identify, you know, where to go, things like that.

Yeah, I’ve been seeing an influx of reports of housing conditions as one of the main issues that people are really afraid to mention, that– their status, but they’re living in really deplorable conditions because of it, and so I just want to make sure that we’re doing everything that we can to track those 311 calls, especially when it’s heat, hot water related, all of those things, because there may be underlying issues that are not specifically talked about as immigration-related issues, but it could definitely be a part of it. I’m going to go over one last topic before I open it up to my colleagues who are here, because I know that they have some time. But I wanted to talk a little bit about the immigrant survivors of domestic violence. Between 34 to 50 percent of immigrant women in the US have experienced domestic violence. This figure increases to 77 percent for immigrant women who use immigrant status– whose immigrant status is dependent upon their spouse. You know, they have really experienced a lot of gender-based violence at extremely high rate. Given that

survivors of gender-based violence are at an incredible vulnerable subset of the immigrant population, how do you prioritize supporting that specific demographic?

Thank you, Chair. In my last hearing, and I think I mentioned this up top as well, one of my current priorities is to really increase our policy teams capacity to expand reach of our efforts. Our office is a member of the Brooklyn Human Trafficking Taskforce, and so through this we are engaging with other city and state stakeholders around servicing this population. We are also in close communication with the Mayor’s Office to End Gender-based Violence on really a variety of topics, but we are actively looking for ways to expand work with specifically this population as well.
And I’d also like to add, the other subset, the LGBTQIA+ community as well. Can you give me a little bit about what you’ve worked on there?

So, this, you know, we’re very excited to work with Director Taylor Brown [sp?] of the new Mayor’s Office of LGBTQIA Affairs. This is another area, Chair, that we are hoping to

really increase our work and explore more partnership.
I encourage that.

If I may add, Commissioner? There was also a Local Law that was passed last year. I’m forgetting the number, but MOIA’s also working with– in consultation with MOERJ to conduct an assessment right now in regards to resources in gaps for transgender, nonconforming and non-binary folks. So that’s work that’s ongoing right now. I would also say with the new roll out of the legal support centers, there are also providers there that are increasing touchpoints with folks who self-identify, and that’s another area that we’re also exploring and working on.
That’s great. And so I’m going to pause there to give my colleagues an opportunity, but I’ll be back. So, Council Member Schulman?

Thank you very much. And I just want to say it’s really nice to see the Commissioner here, and I couldn't think of anybody better to fill that role, so congratulations

and look forward to working with you. And so, a couple of questions I have. One is, there was a report recently about taskforces in different agencies around the sanctuary city law, is that new staff? Is that– is there extra money for that? I’m just curious how that's going to work.
Yeah. I believe you’re referring to the Interagency Response Committee that came from the Executive Order–
[interposing] Okay.

that was signed by mayor, Executive Order 13. That taskforce is a combination of both the FDM’s office, the Special Chief– the Chief Counsel’s office. MOIA has a leadership role at the table as well. In terms of staffing, I believe that is outside of MOIA, but it’s something that our– the special advisor to the FDM is currently working on. I will say that we are in close communication and working very collaboratively with our partners on the

When it’s finalized, if you can get us that information, that would be great. Also, I know you talked about– you

have a comms director, and I know you talked about earned media. Do you have any paid media that you do?
So, we are currently exploring a Know Your Rights campaign that will include a combination of both paid and unpaid ads that will dispersed throughout the city.

So, the question I have– so, as you know, ICE has been dispersed to the city’s airports as part of the TSA issue, whatever. The problem is my understanding is that the airports are kind of exempt from the sanctuary city law, is that correct? The reason I’m asking is, is there any kind of campaign or thought about identifying people that would be traveling or potentially traveling that we could also make sure that they know their rights? Because today there was a woman that was picked up by TSA, pointed out– not here, in San Francisco– to ICE agents and arrested and sent back to Guatemala with her little kid.
So, our sanctuary city laws, you know, are limited to city agencies.
Right.

And how we, you know, cooperate with immigration enforcement, and it– and the limitations around that. I will say that we are concerned with the reports that we’re hearing of ICE agents that have been confirmed at airports. In fact, MOIA did release an advisory just yesterday just to inform travelers on what to expect and give– and provide tips on how to travel safely if they are engaging at the airports.

And I’d like to see, like, community-based organizations that know about some of these people who are traveling or having plans to or whatever, because we don't want people to fall through the cracks.

No, we agree. We pushed out our advisory both on our social media channels but also to our contracted providers through a newsletter announcement that went out to ensure that CBOs who are working with these vulnerable communities have the information that they need.
Because especially at La Guardia Airport which is basically the airport we’re talking about, that–
[interposing] Yeah.
And JFK, there’s a ton of immigrants that go through all the time. With that, Chair, I’m done. But thank you very much, Commissioner.
Thank you.
Thank you. Really quickly, the media advisory that was put out, what languages was that put out in, do you know?
Yeah, we can get that for you.
Okay. I’m having a lot of questions about which languages. Okay. I’d like to now recognize Council Member Brewer.

Thank you very much, and congratulations. So, a couple of things. When we were across the street, the Budget Commissioner stated when asked about which agencies are working on immigration, because people were concerned, he pointed to you and said that you’re coordinating it all. How is that happening? Was it– then he went to the next question.
I have very mighty–
[interposing] So, my question to you, is it through the taskforces? Is it through the 64 people? How do you keep all the agencies that are working on this focused on the issues that are so important?

Yeah. Council Member, thank you for that question. It is a tall task for a five-foot-two woman. It’s a challenge, but I will say that we accomplished all this work. Really the unsung heroes are the staff and the team at MOIA who have been here working diligently long hours, 24 hours a day, working with our contracted providers. So, I want to first and foremost acknowledge the tem at MOIA, and I’m happy to be joined by many of them here. And it’s our contracted providers. These are folks that we contract, organizations, CBOs who are– I know come from these communities, who service these communities that really do and provide the important work of whether it’s legal services, language services. It takes quite literally a village.
Okay, so that– but that, I think– I agree with that. But I think he was talking about the other agency, so that’s also part of what you’re talking about?
So, the agency–
[interposing] I can give you– you all know. You know, Department of Education, Department of Health, the list goes on.

Right. And we mentioned there are a couple– there are a few different avenues where we work with other agencies. The interagency taskforce is one where, you know, we have partnerships across the board. You know, we provide policy updates. We get– we share best practices, that is one avenue. And then we have individual projects. I know– I’ll turn it over to my colleague to talk about some of the partnerships that we have with the

Thank you, Commissioner. And we mentioned this briefly in the last hearing as well, but we are working with the Department of Education and we incorporated one of our programs into the school. So we are working with them on the Rapid Response Collaborative in schools, and what it is, it’s a dedicated touchpoint for students, parents, and/or immediate family members who might live with said student to access legal

services. We work with Project Open Arms which is a dedicated team at the Department of Education.
I’m familiar with them. We’d like the Commissioner to come to District Three April 15th or May 13th, open arms, District Three– largest one. Keep going, sorry.

No. But just to talk a little bit about the model and the work that we’re doing– there is a centralized touchpoint to connect said people to services if they’re at imminent risk of detention or if they were detained. In addition to that, we have also created programs for Know Your Rights that are dedicated to three groups of people directly to students who might be impacted. So you can think about some young people ages 16 to 20 who might be in school. A pocket of– another set of Know Your Rights training for parents, and then a third subset is for educators, parent coordinators and the such, and that's work that’s been ongoing, and I would say, you know, pretty successful–

[interposing] The reason I bring it up also, I go to all the budget hearings, and then I pick up pieces. So, Learning to

Work is an example at District 79. I happen to live with a whole bunch of these migrants and asylum-seekers in my house. So I am familiar with all the programs, and one of them, apparently, might be cut. That is so helpful to your population. And number two, at Small Business, at that hearing, we asked because the freaking feds have cut anybody who is an owner, immigrant, small business, can’t get federal money. That’s half of the small businesses in the City of New York. So, the city is going to try through the small business other funds to come up with money. But I’m just saying there’s– every single agency is impacted by this situation with the President. So, that’s why I’m talking about coordination. So, I don’t know if that’s something that you’re working on. I assume you are.
Yeah, that is something that we’re working on with our agency partners, but as well as our partners at

Okay. And then just finally, adult literacy, that’s important for everybody. Doesn’t have to be just this community. But my understanding is the Coalition for Adult Literacy presented a proposal to DYCD for $21 million

for more funding, and I think there is $12 million in the FY27. so, that would be an example that I hope you would advocate for this funding in the new administration. Well, with this administration, with OMB. The reason I say this is these classes are already over subscribed, and I have to say from my experience, adult literacy is the number one issue. If you’re going to get through the GED, if you’re going to get– which is what my crew is trying to do. And if you’re also trying to just get a job. So how are we dealing with adult literacy?
Council Member, I am not familiar with the exact proposal, but we are happy to review that and several back with advocates.
I think the issue is you’re involved unfortunately with everything in terms of these agencies.
We touch a little bit of everything.
Yes.
And we have good partners at agencies who are ready to do the work.
Okay.

And if I can add, [inaudible] with regards to adult literacy, as part of the Preliminary Budget, we have now an additional $1.5 million that was baselined for our English classes, right? So that will also allow us to continue programming. Currently are collaborating with all three library systems in the city, so we have ongoing classes all throughout the five boroughs in multiple library branches in immigrant dense communities.
Thank you very much.

Thank you. I guess, just to piggyback off of Council Member Brewer, I’m trying to figure out if there is a mechanism by which you track all of these– the agencies that you do have contracts with? So, not just through meeting and touching base, but how are we necessarily tracking what they’re doing, what they’re working on, when they’re working on it, if they’ve accomplished the mission, who they’re contracting with? Is all of that funneled through that interagency conversation or is there like some kind of mechanism which that is tracked?

Yeah, I can walk you through some of the work that we’ve been doing on the legal service side. And I think that this is really sort of lessons learned from the last couple of years in regards to new arrivals coming in and really trying to figure out and hone in on how we centralize and streamline services, right? So, we have regular meetings and communication with other agencies that provide legal services for immigration legal services. So, for example, the Department of Social Services, NGBV, DYCD, and I think I always miss one. But we touch base in regards to our new programming so they’re aware of what we’re having. We’re in close communication if there is an RFP that maybe one agency might be thinking about or putting out of lessons learned and target areas in neighborhoods that we’re working with. So that’s very intentional. It happens frequently with legal service provider side. On the English language learning side, we also connect with DYCD, but it’s more based on pedagogy and just sort of best practices to incorporate into our services as well. So, those are two examples that I can share with you now.

And just briefly to add sort of on sort of the more fun part, the administrative piece and contracting. Our contracting agency is the Department of Social Services, and that’s also where really the bulk of the immigration legal services live under HRA. so, we have, you know, a working relationship with that agency. We have the ad goals [sic]. We do work very closely with those teams as well, not only in the programmatic side, but also taking a look at contracts across the board.

Okay, thank you. So, the Preliminary Plan– and now we’re going to switch over to legal services which we just spoke about– includes new funding which we’re very excited to see, $6.7 million in fiscal 26, $21.3 million in fiscal 27, $20.9 million in fiscal 28, $19.2 in fiscal 29. What exactly will this additional funding be used for?

So, we’re very excited about that additional funding. We don’t have– I don’t have the breakdown for all of that funding for legal services. Specifically for MOIA that means that we have now an additional $14.6

million that was baselined, and that’s to fund– to continue funding for our legal support centers as well additional funding for our Rapid Response Legal Collaborative program. So, specifically, you know, for that funding we’re still in the process of finalizing what allocation looks like for next fiscal year, and like I mentioned earlier, you know, one, we’re highly focused on ensuring that there’s continuity in services and also in the medium to long-term working on efficiencies to be able to allocate funding more efficiently.
Are you looking to create new programs at all?
We’re still in the process of evaluating all of that.
Okay. And so given that the funding is baselined, will there be new RFPs that go on for any of these new programmings? Is that the plan?

You know, we’re still looking at all of our options, right? This funding just got baselined. Right now, most immediately we want to– we want continuity of services, but again, nothing is off the table, you

know, as we plan– as we finalize planning for medium and longer term.

Okay. And so now I’m going to switch a little to start talking about our city’s sanctuary policies, something that we had our first hearing on. We’ll continue to talk about it. There’ll continue to be legislation about it, but on February 6th the Mayor issued Executive Order 13 to strengthen the city’s sanctuary protections, right, and that primarily barring ICE agents from entering city-owned properties without a judicial warrant. Can you provide an update on the interagency response committee that was established pursuant to that Executive Order?

Chair, before I get to that question, I want to go back to your question around languages for the advisory. So, so far, the English is being translated into the top 10 languages, and we will also include Hindi and Punjabi, and those are expected to go up as soon as possible. To your question on the interagency response committee, so you know, it is a response by– a crisis response body that coordinates and manages policy responses across city agencies during a

crisis. Any crisis, but it also includes escalating federal immigration action. So, the members of the committee, as I’ve stated before, the First Deputy Mayor who’s going to be serving as Chair, the Chief Counsel, Special Advisor for Strategic Coordination and Operations for the FDM, and myself. As MOIA’s Commissioner, I am serving in a leadership capacity at the IRC and we’re working really closely with this team.
And how often does it meet? Is it quarterly as well?

So, the Interagency Response Committee right now is actively sort of in communication and working in coordination with the city agencies to meet some of the earlier deadlines. I know that’s– a focus has been largely placed on the May 7th aligned for the audit. So, we know that that work has begun. The IRC is also beginning to meet with stakeholders actually this week. So, that work is– has commenced.
Okay. I’m going to take a pause acknowledge my colleague Council Member Joseph, and she’ll ask you some questions.

Oh, wow, I like that. Okay, okay. Good afternoon, everyone. Commissioner, always great to see you. Thank you for being here, and on the record just also want to thank the administration for the great partnership we did on the TPS video done by the Mayor. I thank him for that. We want to talk about HRA. I know it was baselined. We want to find out are there going to be an expansion, or is there going to be a Haitian-led organization. As you know, TPS is currently now in the Supreme Court.

I think you meant, HRI, the Haitian Response Initiative. We are currently part of what the Commissioner laid out a little bit earlier is that we’re currently assessing all programs to see where the new funding that we received will be allocated, so that’s part of the assessment as well with
Okay. How many organizations do you currently have in the HRI system?

We have– give me one second, just finding my– get my page. We

have eight. So it’s seven CBOs and then Catholic Charities that provides services, legal services.

Okay. And the Preliminary Plan included $1.6 million in fiscal 2026 for the HRA. For fiscal 2026, the Council added an additional $600,000 in discretionary funding to further support six Haitian-serving not-for-profit organizations. Can you provide an update on this program, including the number of people served in 2025?
So, for the Council’s additional funding, I don’t have that number. And for the program that we oversee, in FY26, 333 individuals have been screen and 120 cases have been filed.
And what is the projected budget for the Haitian Response Initiative in 2027?
It has been baselined as of this fiscal year at $1.6 million.

Have the needs of the Haitian community shifted or evolved in the past year? We know it has. We have 300- I’ve done videos. I’ve been outside rallying and doing press

conference as 350,000 lives are looming, because now we’re waiting for a decision. Any other plans to support the community in helping maybe change some of their statuses?

Yeah, there’s– that’s a great question and something we’ve been thinking a lto about. Part of what we’ve done to tackle some of the issues, particularly with the looming or potential end of TPS, is that we have shifted to move the services. Currently, what we are doing– well, one, we’re bringing clinics into a neighborhood so they are now– and this is during FY26 we’ve made that change where they’re coming into the CBOs directly, as well as supporting individuals who might be having questions that are being prepared, as well as we’re currently working on providing resources. We know that TPS looming, there are a lot of issues that have come up regarding housing, work, and things like that. So there are resources that we’re currently producing and putting together for that community as well.

Even in terms of guardianship as well as children who are born here and parents who may have to leave and all of that

stuff. I know I hosted a session in my– in a neighboring district on that.

Yes. So, we have– just generally we have standby guardianship information for the general public on our website, but in addition to what we do with the HRI collaborative, part of it is also training. So we also have Catholic Charities come in and provide updates regarding– which are really a reflection of the most common themes and issues that the organizations are facing, and that was one of them as well.

Thank you. And also wanted to ask around– I know you know this is going to come– around young people. One of the things we did in this last year’s budget is support unaccompanied minors. Is that going to continue? And how many young people have you seen in that program?

So, in regards to whether there will be programming changes, we’re still, again, identifying gaps in needs. And then I do have a number for you, but I’m just looking for it in my binder, in regards to the work. And

really thanks to the Council, too, for providing funding–
[interposing] We were steadfast on that.
That’s right, and we’re very thankful. But in regards to– if you can give me a minute, I’ll get it.

Yeah, no problem. No problem. Meanwhile I can ask another question. Chair, is it okay? Thank you. The Council also funded Literacy Assistance Centers, and ICARE for both CBOs to coordinate and provide technical assistance to providers funded under the adult literacy forward initiative, and those fundings under the SIJS, Unaccompanied Minors and Family initiative, which total $733,000 in the fiscal 2026 for these program. Can you provide details about the use of that funding, and what does these programs, mentorship, assistance and coordination entail, and what is the goal of the funding?

For that, we’re going to have to circle back, because we don’t manage those programs, so we don’t have specifics,

but we’re happy to look into that in follow-up [inaudible].
You’ll work– you’ll work with the other agency to make sure–
[interposing] Yeah, we’ll–
H+H.
Yes.

Is the amount of funding that we provided for The Door to support young people whether they’re in the foster care, whether they are in unaccompanied minors, or whether they are asylum-seekers as well, enough to support the young people that we have? As you can see, dealing after 10 months and Muktar is out now. So we want to continue to support young people. As we’re reading reports, immigration had become the most dangerous thing to young people in this city.

Yeah. And as part of our process between Preliminary and the Executive is to actually evaluate some of these programs and see where the gaps in opportunities are and work with our partners in OMB to address some of those needs.

And is there any other agencies that we’re doing interagency work with? You know, I think other agencies should be talking like me at city public schools, DYCD. There should be interagency conversation about a comprehensive plan for our young people in this city.

I can jump in here. We are in active conversations with DYCD, ACS, and the Department of Education on issues regarding youth and then to give you the number because I found it– as you talked about it sort of– the funding that came in from City Council, we don’t have clear oversight on that in numbers, but I could share in regards to numbers that we supported with the transition of the asylum application– application help center and young people that were supported. There’s a list of about 200 youth who needed continued legal services and ultimately 69 youth were assisted with SIJ applications. That number– what htat number is is because we also had to get consent form young people to actually follow up. So I just wanted to share that number. And one more thing, because the team is pinging me, we’re also working on putting together a family preparedness phoen bank

that would– that’s happening this month in collaboration with Catholic Charities. Actually, next month.
Well, thank you. Thank you very much for this. Chair, thank you so much.

Of course. Thank you. And you know– so I know that a lot of the conversation has been around those interagency conversations, taskforce conversations. Is there a quality check that MOIA does to see that that information has trickled down to the people that are on the ground, and that those conversations or the things that those agencies have said that they are going to give information on, that that’s actually reaching the people that are facing our immigrant communities?

Yeah. Outside of our quarterly meetings for the interagency taskforces, our team are in regular communications. I’ll say that I'll lift one team in particular, our language access folks are in constant communication whether it’s, you know, DYCD, DOE. We had a strong meeting and conversations with our partners at NYCEM just to

ensure that these aren’t just sort of one-off, you know, meetings or translations that happened, but that language access is actually bendy in the work that they do. So, I feel confident in those conversations. They happen outside of not just within the taskforces, but they happen on a regular basis outside as well.

Alright, great. And so when– back to the sanctuary city laws. I was wondering if there were any recommendations that MOIA is providing to the city agencies to ensure compliance with the sanctuary policies. And if you can talk a little bit about what that timeframe is looking like to conduct trainings that are related to Executive Order 13 across all of the relevant agencies?

One thing I think is really important to kind of restate and be unequivocal about is that this administration is in fact committed to ensuring that no city agencies are cooperating with ICE in ways that violate our laws. So, I want to put that on the record. And you know, that commitment we know is not just in words, but it was codified in the Executive Order that lays out

very clear accountability measures for agencies. You know, to the question about trainings, we’re really hoping to uncover is– through the audits is a better understanding of what the training capacity right now looks like. We imagine that, you know, there will be some gaps and we’re looking forward to evaluating those. And in terms of timeline, agencies do have up until I believe it’s May 7th to submit those reports. So we’re hoping to evaluate those and put out recommendations. You know, transparency is really important and so the recommendations will be posted on our website.
So, you anticipate that all city agencies will be trained to some degree even with the gaps that exist, or are you assessign the gaps to see which ones will and won’t?

We are planning to assess the gaps first, and then move forward with our series of recommendations, but there is a commitment for sure to make sure all city agencies are trained, and know exactly how to, you know, interact with the public, how to interact with agencies that know their responsibilities under the sanctuary city law.
Can you describe a little bit about your model for rapid response outreach. I know you spoke about it a bit, but maybe talk a little bit more in depth about the model for rapid response.

Yeah. It's really two-fold. I’ll start with sort of looking in-house within MOIA. One of the things that I really would like to sort of see reflected in some of the changes within MOIA is a more robust rapid response capacity that we have. You know, that means building sort of stronger systems. That means faster coordination with our legal service providers, and also training some of our own staff. You know, we have a number of– I believe it’s 10 community liaisons right now that I really would like to see trained as organizers who can,you know, go out into the community should there be a need, and work with our partners on the ground. We also have a dedicated team that is providing information to the community through our external affairs and community engagement work. These folks are out. They’re tabling. They’re conducting really important Know Your Rights trainings and working really closely with our

partners. So, that's sort of on the in-house side. You know, externally, the great work of our providers is– I think can’t be overstated. You know, the folks who manage our rapid response legal support hotline, you know, they’re– the Rapid Response Legal Support Centers, but our hotline as well– I mentioned this in our testimony, the staffing capacity has expanded and there is a dedicated person specifically for any rapid response concerns that may arise. So, it is a all-of-the-above approach to rapid response.

Thank you for that. I mean, I think that that’s one of the things like even on the ground in my community there are many, many community members that want to get involved, and some items are forming their own rapid response networks. It’s very difficult for them to get proper education, make sure that they’re doing correctly, so that we are not kind of chasing our tails in a moment of extreme need.
